storylines.label: Fast Inference
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Warmctl – Fast cold starts for vLLM inference

editorial.tldr: This is a loose cluster of three unrelated projects that share one goal: serving LLMs faster below the model layer. It began with Resin, a native scheduler for inference engines, and was followed by Hibana, an arXiv paper on agentic inference for unified-memory devices.
editorial.whats_new: Warmctl, a new open-source tool shared on Show HN, targets slow cold starts for vLLM servers, adding a startup-latency fix to a thread about scheduling and local serving.
editorial.why_it_matters: Inference latency increasingly depends on the layers around the model (request scheduling, memory layout, server warm-up), and each of these projects targets one of those layers.
editorial.take_for_builders: If vLLM startup time limits your autoscaling, measure your current cold-start time first, then trial Warmctl on a non-production replica and compare.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Coder Arrives at 775 GB, Built to Fit One GPU

editorial.tldr: Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro surfaced after Arena testing on Oct 23 and launched Oct 24 as a roughly 3T-parameter API flagship, then a botched launch forced a quota reset and apology. The Hugging Face listing appeared Nov 2, full 1.56TB weights were reported Nov 5, and vLLM, Huawei Ascend and Moore Threads added serving and fine-tuning support.
editorial.whats_new: A Kimi K3.1 Pro Coder variant has arrived at 775 GB and is reported to fit on one GPU, about half the size of the 1.56TB full checkpoint.
editorial.why_it_matters: A coding-focused 775 GB variant lowers the hardware bar for self-hosting a frontier-class open-weight coder, while the full Pro model still needs a large multi-accelerator cluster.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you want a self-hosted open-weight coding model, evaluate the 775 GB Coder variant on your own coding evals before sizing a cluster for the 1.56TB Pro, and check the license conditions first.

status.detail: Weights are public with conditional commercial use, engine and accelerator support is spreading, and a smaller Coder variant now targets single-GPU deployment.

storylines.label: Closing Gap
storylines.latest_title: Closing the AI guidance gap in education

editorial.tldr: This is not one developing story: three unrelated items share only the phrase "closing the gap" in their titles. Two October arXiv papers target model-side gaps, KV-cache memory in looped transformers and the CLIP-style modality gap in embeddings.
editorial.whats_new: OpenAI published ThinkYoung research and EMEA education-partnership lessons on AI literacy for teachers, an education-policy piece with no technical link to the earlier papers.
editorial.why_it_matters: Only the KV-sharing paper bears on inference cost: looped architectures multiply KV-cache memory per recurrence, which sets serving footprint if they reach production.
editorial.take_for_builders: Nothing to change: treat these as three separate reads, and keep the KV-sharing paper on file only if you evaluate looped or recurrent-depth models for serving.

storylines.label: Inference GPUs
storylines.latest_title: CUDA+ROCm dual-back ends LLM inference for mixed-vendor GPUs (up to 48% faster)

editorial.tldr: This is a loose thread of three separate projects, not one event: each tries to run inference on GPUs beyond a single CUDA stack. Google opened it with ML Drift, an Apache 2.0 engine for on-device inference across GPU vendors, and a small C++/HIP inference server for AMD GPUs followed on Codeberg.
editorial.whats_new: A pull request to the open-source project-maya adds combined CUDA and ROCm backends so one LLM inference job can span NVIDIA and AMD GPUs; its title claims up to 48% faster, with no independent benchmark yet.
editorial.why_it_matters: Inference that runs on more than one GPU vendor gives teams leverage on hardware cost and supply, but these projects are early and their performance numbers are self-reported.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as experiments: rerun your own latency and throughput evals on mixed or AMD hardware before you plan capacity around them, and keep your CUDA serving path as the fallback.

storylines.label: NVIDIA Nemotron
storylines.latest_title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

editorial.tldr: NVIDIA's open Nemotron family widened on Oct 28 with Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2 for promptable multilingual transcription. A day later AWS published a guide to running the 120B-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS.
editorial.whats_new: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter multimodal model, is now a managed option in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, deployable as an NVFP4 or BF16 variant.
editorial.why_it_matters: Nemotron 3.5 now has two AWS deployment paths, self-managed Kubernetes (EKS, HyperPod EKS) and managed JumpStart, plus a speech model, so an open-weight stack can be trialed without building serving infrastructure first.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run multimodal agents on AWS, deploy both the NVFP4 and BF16 Super VL variants from JumpStart against your own eval set and compare cost and accuracy before choosing one.

status.detail: Nemotron 3.5 has moved from model releases to packaged deployment on AWS, with Super VL now in JumpStart.

storylines.label: Learning Adaptive
storylines.latest_title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels

editorial.tldr: This is not one developing event: three unrelated arXiv papers share the word "adaptive" and one idea, spending scarce resources where they help most. LAND (Nov 2) varies Best-of-N draws per input, and ASP (Nov 6) schedules RL rollouts to cut idle GPU time.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 9 theory paper shows adaptive quantization keeps TD learning's fast convergence rate even when an agent's updates cross a rate-limited channel.
editorial.why_it_matters: Each paper targets a different budget: inference samples (LAND), RL-training GPU utilization (ASP), and communication bandwidth (TD quantization); only the first two touch production LLM stacks today.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run Best-of-N or async RL, read LAND and ASP for per-input sample budgets and rollout scheduling; treat the TD paper as theory, not a deployment change.

storylines.label: Reasoning Multimodal
storylines.latest_title: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents

editorial.tldr: Late-October arXiv papers worked on getting reasoning into multimodal models: reasoning-augmented embeddings, rewardable perception, latent vision-to-small-model communication and continuous-space reasoning. Early November turned to reliability (refusal, perception robustness, hallucination) and then to post-release unlearning and knowledge editing.
editorial.whats_new: Two Nov 9 papers move the thread toward agents: HumanSightBench tests the human-easy visual questions MLLMs still miss, and HiVe-Mem proposes a memory system for multimodal agents with long interaction histories.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multimodal reasoning research now targets what agent builders hit in production: perception errors, unsupported answers, stale knowledge and retrieval over long multimodal histories.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run multimodal agents, add evals for insufficient-evidence refusal, perceptual perturbation and long-history retrieval before adopting any of these techniques; treat them as preprints until reproduced.

status.detail: A loose cluster of arXiv preprints on multimodal reasoning, moving from adding reasoning toward reliability, maintenance and agent memory; none is an independently reproduced result.

storylines.label: Anomaly Detection
storylines.latest_title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection

editorial.tldr: This thread is a label, not one event: four unrelated arXiv papers that share the words "anomaly detection". The October pair targeted video and few-shot industrial inspection, and the August papers it replaced covered relational data, ICS security and streaming video.
editorial.whats_new: Two Nov 9 papers push anomaly detection toward cheaper inference: LogCDM flags log anomalies from behavioral-graph drift without GPU-bound language models, and Vendi Anomaly Scores proposes a diversity-based score in place of density or isolation heuristics.
editorial.why_it_matters: The shared direction is cost: three of the four papers explicitly target cheaper or lighter detection than dense VLM, exemplar-store or 8B-parameter log models, which is the constraint that decides whether a detector can run inside a monitoring or agent pipeline.
editorial.take_for_builders: Read LogCDM if your log anomaly detection needs GPU-hosted models today; skip the rest unless you run video or visual inspection, and wait for released code before planning a swap.

storylines.label: Multi-agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

editorial.tldr: The thread opened Oct 21-22 with production write-ups (AWS Deep Insight, DoorDash flag cleanup) and a paper on herding cascades in multi-agent LLM systems, followed by a run of arXiv benchmarks and training, memory and orchestration methods for long-horizon agents. From Nov 1 the focus turned to the evals themselves: task depth, non-English tool use, LLM-judge drift and single-run variance.
editorial.whats_new: Two Nov 9 benchmarks put agents on operator work: Infrathon tests long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization, and WorkflowArena scores multi-agent systems on producing executable workflow orchestrations.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multi-agent and long-horizon agent results are only as useful as the eval behind them, and the newest benchmarks now target infra tuning and workflow orchestration, the work platform teams would actually hand an agent.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before giving an agent infra or orchestration work, run the task several times and report the spread, and recheck any LLM judge in your eval against fresh human labels.

status.detail: A broad research cluster on multi-agent and long-horizon agents, now converging on benchmarks for infrastructure and orchestration work and on whether existing evals measure what they claim.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning

editorial.tldr: This thread is a running stream of reinforcement-learning preprints, not one event; it was reclustered from a broader LLM-knowledge reading list. From Oct 21 the papers moved from agentic RL over stateful environments and credit assignment to training-stack fixes, then to multi-agent and long-horizon web agents in early November.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 9: the MaxIM preprint trains incremental summarization with RL so an agent keeps a bounded memory of an unbounded interaction history, optimized for downstream task utility.
editorial.why_it_matters: RL is becoming the default post-training tool for agents, and these papers locate where it breaks: credit assignment across turns, inference/training numeric mismatch, rollout cost and memory limits.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before running RL post-training on an agent, check that your inference and training engines produce matching log-probs, and size rollout budgets against the Nov 4 depth/breadth findings; treat the rest as unreplicated preprints.

storylines.label: On-Policy Distillation
storylines.latest_title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks

editorial.tldr: On Oct 22 an arXiv paper asked when a student trained on its own sampled outputs should follow its teacher, a refinement of on-policy distillation (OPD). By Oct 30 papers had applied OPD to multi-agent routing and to rerankers, and on Nov 8 one measured how much quantized or asynchronous rollout mismatch OPD tolerates.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 9: Agentic-OPD, an arXiv paper, argues that keeping only the best-validation checkpoint from GRPO agent training discards capabilities, and uses on-policy distillation to recover them.
editorial.why_it_matters: On-policy distillation is moving from a training trick into agent post-training and serving components, and its rollout cost now has a studied trade-off against quantized or asynchronous inference.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you RL-train agents with GRPO, keep intermediate checkpoints instead of only the best-validation one until Agentic-OPD's recovery results are reproduced; none of these papers has independent replication yet.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Large Language Models as a Universal Searcher for Open-World Automated Machine Learning

editorial.tldr: This is not one story: the items share the phrase "large language models" and are mostly arXiv papers from Oct 21 onward. Two real threads sit inside it: the Mistral Large 4 launch on Oct 29, and a run of papers on how LLMs and agents handle memory, retrieval, and knowledge updates.
editorial.whats_new: The Nov 9 additions are two arXiv papers, a personality-influence benchmark and an LLM-as-AutoML-searcher, so no new event has landed since Mistral Large 4 got day-0 vLLM and Hugging Face support on Oct 29.
editorial.why_it_matters: The only deployable change here is Mistral Large 4 on vLLM; the memory and retrieval papers are research signal for agent context design, not shipped tooling.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you serve open weights, test Mistral Large 4 on a current vLLM build before adopting it; treat the memory and retrieval papers as design input for your context layer, not drop-in components.
